topic.title: Learning from Incomplete and Indirect Labels
topic.overview: Supervision can specify less than a full correct label: a class may be ruled out, one positive category may be named, or only group-level proportions may be known. This topic develops learning objectives that use those weaker signals while accounting for the information they omit.
topic.whyItMatters: Cheaper annotations can broaden access to training data, but missingness is often selective. Treating an unmentioned category as negative or assuming annotations are random can introduce systematic errors that more data alone cannot remove.
topic.evolution: Early representatives combine labeled and unlabeled observations or group examples into multiple instances. Later work learns from complementary labels, rankings, and proportions. Recent analyses emphasize annotation salience and general-loss guarantees. The common evolution is toward explicitly modeling the annotation process, while the different weak-label settings retain distinct identifiability conditions.
openQuestions: Which annotation biases can be estimated without fully labeled validation data?
How should different weak supervision types be combined without double-counting evidence?
